title: Fortified Wines in Depth
description: Sherry, Port and Madeira in full: production, styles, ageing and how to read them.
L: Explain the chemistry of stopping fermentation

Fortifying spirit is grape spirit, usually distilled to between 77 and 96%. Port uses aguardente at about 77%, which carries some flavour of its own. Sherry and most vins doux naturels use neutral spirit at around 95 to 96%, which adds alcohol without flavour. Less spirit is needed when it's stronger.

Yeast can't work above about 15 to 16% alcohol. Adding spirit mid-fermentation pushes the wine past that point, killing the yeast and keeping the remaining sugar. In Port, about 115 litres of spirit go into 435 litres of fermenting must, making the classic 550-litre pipe. The earlier the spirit goes in, the sweeter the wine.
Why does adding spirit mid-fermentation keep a wine sweet?
The higher alcohol kills the yeast before it finishes
Yeast stops working above about 15 to 16% alcohol, leaving the unfermented sugar.

Spirit added early gives sweet, fruity wines: Port, vins doux naturels and sweet Madeira. Added late, after a dry fermentation, it gives dry wines: Fino, Manzanilla, Sercial Madeira. Each family also uses ageing, with or without oxygen, to shape the final style.
Match each wine to when spirit is added.
Timing determines sweetness; strength determines whether flor can grow.
Fortifying spirit ranges from 77% for Port to about 96% for Sherry
Spirit above about 16% alcohol stops the yeast
Early fortification keeps sugar; late fortification keeps the wine dry
Explain the solera system in detail

Flor is a film of Saccharomyces yeasts that grows on wine in barrels filled only to about five-sixths, leaving air space. It needs 15 to 15.5% alcohol, cool, humid cellars and nutrients. It consumes oxygen, alcohol and glycerol, and produces acetaldehyde, which gives Fino its tangy, nutty, bready aroma. Flor is thickest in spring and autumn.
Flor feeds on air, alcohol and glycerol

The solera system blends wines of different ages. Wine for bottling, the saca, is taken from the oldest scale, the solera. It is refilled from the first criadera, which is refilled from the second, and so on, an operation called rocío. By law, no more than 40% can be drawn per year. Older wine educates the younger; the average age rises over time.
Flor needs barrels to be completely full to grow.
Not true. Barrels are left about five-sixths full so flor has air on the surface to grow.

Sherry must be aged in Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María or Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Sanlúcar, by the mouth of the Guadalquivir, is coolest and most humid, so flor grows thickest there; its Fino is called Manzanilla. Albariza soil, up to 40% chalk, stores winter rain for dry summers.
Why is flor thickest in Sanlúcar de Barrameda?
Its cool, humid sea air favours flor
Coastal humidity and cooler temperatures keep flor thick, giving Manzanilla its saline freshness.
Flor needs air space, 15% alcohol and humid cellars
The solera draws from the oldest scale and refills from younger ones

Fino and Manzanilla age under flor, biological ageing, giving pale, dry, tangy wines at 15%. Oloroso is fortified to 17%, never has flor and ages oxidatively, turning dark brown with walnut, toffee and spice, yet stays dry. As water evaporates, Olorosos concentrate, reaching 20% or more.
Fino under flor; Oloroso with air

Amontillado starts as Fino under flor, then the flor dies or is killed by fortifying to about 17%, and the wine ages oxidatively. It combines Fino's tang with Oloroso's nuttiness. Palo Cortado is rare: it starts under flor but loses it early, then ages oxidatively, giving Amontillado's aroma with Oloroso's body.
Match each Sherry to its ageing.
Biological and oxidative ageing create the range of dry Sherries.

Pedro Ximénez grapes are dried in the sun until almost raisins, then fortified, giving black, syrupy wines with over 400 g/l of sugar. Moscatel is made similarly. Cream Sherry blends Oloroso with sweet wine; Pale Cream blends Fino with sweetening. These blends are sweet; the dry styles are not.
Cream Sherry is sweetened. Fino, Oloroso and Amontillado are naturally dry.
Fino and Manzanilla age under flor; Oloroso ages with air
Amontillado and Palo Cortado combine both
Pedro Ximénez and Cream are sweet styles
Explain the Douro's role in Port

Port grapes grow in the Douro's three sub-regions: the Baixo Corgo, coolest and wettest; the Cima Corgo, heart of quality; and the Douro Superior, hottest and driest. Vineyards are classified A to F. The wine traditionally travelled down to the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across from Porto, for cool, humid ageing.
Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo, Douro Superior

Ruby Ports age in large vats, with little oxygen, keeping colour and fruit. Reserve Ruby is a better selection. Tawny Ports age in small 550-litre casks, called pipes, where oxygen turns them brown and nutty. Aged tawny with an indication of age, 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years, is a blend tasted to match that style. Colheita is a single-vintage tawny.
Vats for ruby; pipes for tawny
A tawny from a single vintage
Colheita is a single-vintage tawny aged at least 7 years in cask.

White Port, from white grapes like Malvasia Fina and Gouveio, ranges from dry to sweet; mixed with tonic, it's a classic aperitif in Porto. Rosé Port, approved in 2008, is made with short skin contact and drunk young and chilled. Aged white Ports, with age indications, also exist.
Match each Port to its ageing.
Ageing in vat or cask defines the family.
Port grapes grow in the Douro's three sub-regions
Ruby ages in large vats; tawny in small casks
Colheita is a single-vintage tawny; white and rosé Ports exist
Explain how a vintage is declared
Compare Vintage, single quinta and LBV
Explain how to serve Vintage Port

Vintage Port is made only in exceptional years, declared by each house, typically about three times a decade. The wine must be approved by the IVDP, the Port institute, and bottled after two to three years. It then ages in bottle for decades. Classic declared years include 1963, 1977, 1994, 2011 and 2017.

In good but not great years, houses may release single quinta vintage Ports from one estate, like Quinta do Vesuvio. Late Bottled Vintage, LBV, comes from a single year, bottled after 4 to 6 years in wood, so it's ready earlier. Unfiltered LBV can age further and throw a sediment.
Vintage Port is bottled after two to three years and ages mainly in bottle.
Yes. That's why it keeps dark colour and fruit for decades and throws a heavy sediment.
Stand a Vintage Port upright for a day, then decant it slowly. Young vintages benefit from a few hours of air; very old ones should be drunk soon after decanting.
What distinguishes LBV from Vintage Port?
LBV spends 4 to 6 years in wood before bottling
Longer time in wood makes LBV ready earlier, unlike Vintage, which ages in bottle.
Vintage Port is declared only in exceptional years
Single quinta Ports come from one estate in good years
LBV is aged longer in wood and ready earlier
Explain estufagem and canteiro in detail
Explain Tinta Negra and the noble grapes

Estufagem heats wine in stainless steel tanks to 45 to 50 degrees for at least three months, then rests it; this is used mainly for younger wines. Canteiro ages wine in casks in warm lofts, called armazéns, for years, sometimes decades. Canteiro is slower and gentler, giving finer, more complex wines. The best Madeiras are all canteiro.
Estufagem: fast heat. Canteiro: slow warmth.

Madeira labels show age: 5 years, called Reserve; 10 years, Special Reserve; 15 years, Extra Reserve; and 20, 30, 40 and 50 years. Colheita is a single vintage aged at least five years. Frasqueira, or Vintage, comes from a single noble grape and year, aged at least 20 years in cask.
What is required for a Frasqueira Madeira?
A single noble grape, a single year and 20 years in cask
Frasqueira is the top category: one grape, one vintage, 20 years minimum in cask.

The noble white grapes, Sercial, Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia, define sweetness when named on the label. Terrantez is a rare fifth. Tinta Negra, a black grape, makes most Madeira; since 2015 its name can appear on labels. Madeira keeps high acidity, with sugar ranging from under 50 g/l in Sercial to over 100 g/l in Malvasia.
Order these Madeira age categories from youngest to oldest.
Each step requires longer ageing; Frasqueira also requires a single grape and year.
Estufagem heats quickly; canteiro ages slowly in warm lofts
Labels show age from 5 years to Frasqueira at 20 or more
Noble grapes define sweetness; Tinta Negra makes most Madeira

Not true. LBV spends 4 to 6 years in wood; Vintage is bottled after two to three.
In Madeira, slow ageing in casks in warm lofts is called ____.
Spirit timing and strength shape each family
Sherry relies on flor, oxygen and the solera
